cases.abstract: ConvNeXt examines whether hierarchical vision Transformers' performance advantages require attention or can be recovered through convolutional design and modern training. Updating the training recipe alone raises ResNet-50 ImageNet-1K top-1 accuracy from 76.1% to 78.8%, establishing a stronger starting point for architectural comparisons. Under this fixed recipe, we progressively modify ResNet to separate spatial and channel mixing, placing large depthwise kernels before channel-expanding pointwise layers and simplifying activation and normalization patterns. The resulting convolutional hierarchy requires neither shifted-window attention nor relative position biases. With ImageNet-1K training at 384 x 384 resolution, ConvNeXt-B reaches 85.1% accuracy versus Swin-B's 84.5%, alongside 12.5% higher inference throughput on a V100 GPU. ConvNeXt-XL reaches 87.8% top-1 accuracy at 384 x 384 resolution after ImageNet-22K pretraining and ImageNet-1K fine-tuning, extending the evaluation beyond the small-model exploration. COCO detection and instance segmentation and ADE20K semantic segmentation likewise match or exceed the evaluated Swin counterparts. These comparisons support modernized convolution as an alternative for the tested recognition tasks, without settling attention's usefulness for multimodal interaction or structured outputs.
cases.methods: ConvNeXt separates spatial filtering from channel mixing so that enlarging the receptive field does not require dense convolution across every channel pair. Each residual block applies a 7 x 7 depthwise convolution before pointwise layers expand the channel dimension fourfold and project it back. Keeping the spatial filter on the narrower representation limits its computational cost, while the dense channel transformations carry most of the work. A single GELU between the pointwise layers and one LayerNorm simplify the block. Separate stride-two convolutions downsample between stages; added normalization at resolution changes stabilizes this otherwise divergent design. These choices are developed through sequential modifications under a fixed 300-epoch AdamW recipe, with roughly controlled FLOPs and accuracy averaged over three seeds in the ResNet-50 regime. This controls the training recipe, but sequential changes and varying intermediate FLOPs do not isolate independent component effects.
cases.results: ConvNeXt-B improves accuracy and measured inference throughput together in the ImageNet-1K-trained, 384 x 384 comparison: 85.1% versus 84.5% top-1 accuracy for Swin-B, and 95.7 versus 85.1 images per second on a V100 GPU. Its competitiveness also extends to dense prediction. With both backbones pretrained on ImageNet-22K, Cascade Mask R-CNN under a 3x schedule yields 54.0 box AP and 46.9 mask AP on COCO for ConvNeXt-B, versus 53.0 and 45.8 for Swin-B. Yet the design trajectory does not support treating every Transformer convention as an improvement: substituting GELU for ReLU alone leaves accuracy unchanged, and increasing kernels beyond 7 x 7 yields no further gain. Separate downsampling initially causes divergence until normalization is added at resolution changes. Thus, the evidence supports the combined design, while making normalization at resolution changes a condition of the reported downsampling result.
cases.notes: Revision preserves the initial training, classification, scaling, and downstream evidence, but connects block ordering to computational cost and treats failed substitutions as evidence about design selection. Roadmap comparisons are sequential, with approximate FLOP control; their effects are not independently additive. The roadmap's 82.0% endpoint and Table 1's 82.1% are distinct. V100 throughput is classification inference, not training speed or detector FPS.

cases.abstract: 3D Gaussian splatting addresses the tension between optimizing a radiance field for image quality and rendering it quickly enough for interactive viewing. A static scene is represented by anisotropic 3D Gaussians initialized from sparse structure-from-motion points, with learnable geometry, opacity, and spherical-harmonic appearance. Because these primitives project directly to image-space splats, the same differentiable rasterizer supports reconstruction and subsequent viewing. Parameter updates alternate with cloning, splitting, and pruning to adapt the representation's density. The tile-based rasterizer shares sorting across pixels and blends splats in approximate depth order, without limiting how many contributing Gaussians receive gradients. Evaluation covers 13 real scenes and bounded synthetic scenes. At 30,000 iterations, real-scene dataset averages reach 134-154 frames per second on an A6000 GPU at their respective native resolutions, after approximately 27-42 minutes of training. The resulting quality exceeds that of the evaluated InstantNGP and Plenoxels configurations and is competitive with Mip-NeRF360, although the latter retains higher PSNR on its own dataset. This combination supports interactive novel-view synthesis, but stores larger models than InstantNGP and Mip-NeRF360 and retains artifacts under sparse view coverage or changing splat order.
cases.methods: The Gaussian rasterizer shares visibility work across pixels to make the same explicit representation practical for optimization and interactive viewing. It partitions the screen into 16 x 16 tiles, duplicates each projected Gaussian across the tiles it overlaps, and sorts the instances once on the GPU using tile identifiers and depth. Tiles load splats into shared memory and blend them front to back until each pixel's opacity saturates. Shared ordering removes per-pixel sorting, but makes blending approximate, particularly for large splats. Backpropagation reuses the sorted tile lists in reverse, recovering intermediate blending quantities from accumulated opacity instead of storing variable-length lists for individual pixels. This permits gradients for every contributing splat without a predetermined count limit. Together, shared sorting and reverse traversal reduce repeated visibility work and storage overhead without truncating gradient propagation solely to keep a fixed splat count.
cases.results: On the Mip-NeRF360 dataset, 30,000-iteration Gaussian splatting improves SSIM to 0.815 and LPIPS to 0.214 against the published reference values of 0.792 and 0.237, respectively, but has lower PSNR: 27.21 versus 27.69 dB. Competitive quality is therefore metric-dependent. Relative to 7,000 iterations, its dataset-average PSNR rises from 25.60 to 27.21 dB, while training increases from 6 minutes 25 seconds to 41 minutes 33 seconds and A6000 rendering falls from 160 to 134 frames per second at native test-image resolutions. Stored parameters grow from 523 to 734 MB, far above Mip-NeRF360's 8.6 MB. In the separate Truck ablation using manually downsampled inputs, limiting gradients to ten splats destabilizes optimization and reduces 30,000-iteration PSNR from 24.81 to 13.84 dB. This failure supports avoiding a fixed gradient cap in the tested optimization. The results support interactive rendering at competitive quality, with model storage and artifacts in poorly observed regions or during splat-order changes still limiting the evaluated system.
cases.notes: The revision keeps the initial quality, training, rendering, memory, and gradient-cap evidence. Table 1's Mip-NeRF360 quality values on its dataset are adopted from the original publication; its training used four A100 GPUs for 12 hours, so no matched A6000 speedup is inferred. Storage means optimized parameters, not peak GPU allocation. Table 3 uses manually downsampled inputs. Successful random initialization in bounded synthetic scenes does not remove the adverse real-scene initialization result.
